      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/israel-med-ny-offensiv-_-tre-drept-1.18084431</link>
      <description>Israels hær sier den har innledet en operasjon i Hamas-kontrollerte områder i Gaza
Israel har innledet en militæroperasjon i det sentrale Gaza vest for den såkalte gule linjen, som har skilt Hamas-kontrollerte og israelsk-kontrollerte områder siden våpenhvilen trådte i kraft i fjor. Det opplyser militæret til AFP.
Vitner sier at israelske stridsvogner rullet inn på hovedveien Salahudeen, vest for den såkalte gule linjen som markerer grensen for de to tredjedelene av Gazastripen som fortsatt er under israelsk kontroll.
Den såkalte gule linjen ble etablert etter våpenhvilen i oktober 2025 og skiller israelskkontrollerte og palestinske soner i Gazastripen. Israelske styrker har gradvis flyttet den gule linjen og utvidet området under direkte militær kontroll i Gaza.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Braathen med ny maktdemonstrasjon: – Jeg er så full av følelser</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sport/braathen-med-ny-maktdemonstrasjon_-_-jeg-er-sa-full-av-folelser-1.18082207</link>
      <description>Norsk-brasilianske Lucas Pinheiro Braathen (26) fortsetter å ydmyke konkurrentene.
Etter seier i storslalåm-starten i Sölden, fortsatte han med seier i slalåm i finske Levi søndag.
– Det er så godt å være her i Levi. Jeg er så full av følelser nå. Jeg skal prøve å ta selvtilliten med meg videre til neste renn, sier Braathen selv i arenaintervjuet.
Clément Noël ble nummer to, 56 hundredeler bak vinneren. Atle Lie McGrath ble beste norske på 7. plass.
– Det er hans bakke. Han elsker den. Han elsker disse forholdene, sier TV 2-ekspert Kjetil Jansrud på direkten.
– Han er fremdeles norsk, men han representerer Brasil. Vi skulle gjerne ha sett det norske flagget bak navnet hans, fortsetter Jansrud.
Dette er den tredje vinteren der Braathen representerer Brasil etter at han brøt med Norges Skiforbund.
– For en kjøring. Det er store, store avstander i en bakke som Levi, sa TV 2-ekspert Jansrud etter Braathens første omgang.
Han ledet med hele 65 hundredeler til toeren, Clément Noël, før finaleomgangen.

– Det Lucas gjør det er helt i egen klasse, sa Timon Haugan til TV 2 etter første omgang.
– Jeg fikk meg en på tygga, sier McGrath om finaleomgangen.
Oscar Andreas Sandvik kjørte seg opp fra 29. plass til nummer 11.
Både Timon Haugan og Henrik Kristoffersen tapte halvannet sekund til Braathen i første omgang. Begge fortsatte å skuffe i andre omgang og ble henholdsvis 18 og 19.
– Jeg kjørte i en stein, forteller Kristoffersen til TV 2.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Vind og kaos-skyting: Kirkeeide vant fellesstarten etter åtte (!) bom</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sport/vind-og-kaos-skyting_-kirkeeide-vant-fellesstarten-etter-atte-___-bom-1.18082184</link>
      <description>Maren Kirkeeide stakk av med seieren på kvinnenes fellesstart i skiskyting på Geilo søndag.
Lørdagens sprintsensasjon Guro Ytterhus imponerte igjen og tok andreplass 14,4 sekunder bak Kirkeeide.
Juni Arnekleiv ledet etter to fulle hus, men på tredje skyting ble det kaos. Sterk vind gjorde at flere av utøverne bommet mange ganger, og Arnekleiv røk på fire bom.
Dermed tok Karoline Knotten over teten. Men på siste skyting, så haglet skuddene utenfor blinkene nok en gang.
Og plutselig var Kirkeeide i tet etter hele åtte (!) bom. Få løpere måtte ut i flere strafferunder, men likevel holdt hun ledelsen helt til mål.
– Det var en merkelig fellesstart. Det var veldig mange som bommet. Det var tydeligvis ikke så lett som man skulle tro, sier Kirkeeide til NRK etter seieren.
Karoline Knotten tok tredjeplass.
Ingrid Landmark Tandrevold, Marthe Kråkstad Johansen, Karoline Knotten og nevnte Kirkeeide er forhåndsuttatt til verdenscupstarten i finske Kontiolahti senere i måneden. Kvinnenes tropp skal til slutt bestå av seks løpere.</description>

      <title>Flystansen i USA: Bytting av kabel mulig årsak</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/flystansen-i-usa_-bytting-av-kabel-mulig-arsak-1.18082036</link>
      <description>USAs transportminister Sean Duffy sier utskiftning av en kobbertråd kan være årsaken til den omfattende flystansen fredag.
Flere enn 15.000 flygninger ble forsinket eller innstilt da amerikanske luftfartsmyndigheter FAA i fire timer nektet alle fly å ta av på grunn av forstyrrelser i flykontrollen.
På en pressekonferanse lørdag sa transportminister Duffy at problemene kan ha oppstått som følge av arbeidet med å bytte ut gamle kobberkabler med fiber ved et av FAAs anlegg.
Ministeren oppgav også navnet på selskapet han mente hadde forsårsaket problemene. Hendelsen skal granskes videre.
Det er fremdeles etterslep etter fredagens problemer. Lørdag er flere enn 10.000 flygninger innstilt eller forsinket, ifølge FlightAware.</description>

      <description>Det brenner kraftig i en enebolig på en gård i Trondheimsveien i Lillestrøm.
– Det er full fyr i hele bygningen, opplyser oppdragsleder i politiet, Ronny Mangseth.
– Brannvesenet er fremme og er i gang med slukking. Det er kontroll på alle fire beboere på stedet, sier han.
Ved 17:20-tiden opplyser politiet at det fortsatt brenner i boligen, og at arbeidet med slukking vil ta tid.
En person skal ha fått i seg noe røyk.
Det skal ikke være fare for spredning til låve eller andre bygninger på gården.
Ifølge politiet er det ikke kjent hva som er årsaken til brannen, og de vil etterforske saken videre.</description>

      <title>Solbakken overrasker – Aasgaard inn i startelleveren</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sport/solbakken-overrasker-_-aasgaard-inn-i-startelleveren-1.18081988</link>
      <description>Ståle Solbakken har valgt ut følgende ellever til kampen mot Wales på Ullevaal:
Egil Selvik – Julian Ryerson, Kristoffer Ajer, Torbjørn Heggem, David Møller Wolfe – Sander Berge, Martin Ødegaard, Thelo Aasgaard – Antonio Nusa, Erling Braut Haaland, Oscar Bobb.
– Jeg må innrømme at jeg er noe overrasket. Men da tenker vel Solbakken at han passer bedre til denne kampen enn det Patrick Berg gjør akkurat nå, sier NRK-ekspert Andrine Hegerberg om at Aasgaards inntog i startelleveren.
Han er én av fire bytter som er gjort fra elleveren som møtte Portugal i forrige nasjonsligakamp.
Leo Østigård, Andreas Schjelderup og Patrick Berg er henvist til benken, mens Fredrik Aursnes ikke er med på grunn av en skade.
Samtidig er det nok en gang Egil Selvik som skal vokte buret for Norge.
– Jeg er først og fremst stolt, men også spent. Det blir en viktig kamp for oss, så det gjelder å gi jernet. Vi har noe å revansjere, sier Selvik til TV 2.
På motsatt banehalvdel starter Wales med følgende mannskap:
Karl Darlow – Neco Williams, Joe Rodon, Ben Davies, Jay Dasilva – Harry Wilson, Ethan Ampadu, Liam Cullen, Daniel James – Lewis Koumas, Brennan Johnson.</description>

      <title>Kjørte ned tre personer</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sorlandet/kjorte-ned-tre-personer--1.18081598</link>
      <description>En eldre kvinnelig bilfører kjørte ned tre personer i Lyngdal.
To personer på sparkesykkel ble truffet av bilen, før den fortsatte og traff en tredje person.
Denne personen ble hentet med ambulanse, mens de to på sparkesykkel fikk mindre skader. Det melder politiet på Agder.
Bilisten er en kvinne i 80-årene, og hun skal ha kjørt bilen opp på fortauet.
Bilen skal også ha vært borti et bygg som har fått skader.</description>

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/britisk-politi-starter-etterforskning-av-david-walliams-1.18081553</link>
      <description>Britisk politi bekrefter overfor BBC at de har innledet en etterforskning mot komikeren David Walliams for alvorlige seksuelle forbrytelser.
Det skjer etter at flere kvinner har stått frem med anklager om at Walliams skal ha brukt kjendisstatusen sin for å tilnærme seg unge kvinner seksuelt.
Ifølge politiet er det ikke disse anklagene som er grunnlaget for etterforskningen.
Walliams er kjent for humorserien «Little Britain» og har de senere årene blant annet gjort seg bemerket som barnebokforfatter.
Han har avvist å ha gjort noe galt.</description>

Mark Carney met with U.S. President Donald Trump in China on a day when the prime minister noted trade talks with Washington are far more complex than the ones Canada is having with Beijing.

The post Carney meets Trump in China, says Canada’s U.S. trade ‘much more complex’ than China appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

Mark Carney met with U.S. President Donald Trump in China on Wednesday, as he also said trade talks with Washington are far more complex than the ones Canada is having with Beijing.

The two leaders had a conversation that lasted just under 20 minutes, Carney’s office said, during what was dinnertime in Shenzhen and the early morning in Canada.

“The leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create good jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty,” according to a readout from Carney’s office.

“They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact.”

Carney’s office said the meeting included U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Trump’s chief of staff Stephen Miller and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Carney’s chief of staff Marc-André Blanchard and Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand were there on the Canadian side.

Shortly before the meeting, Carney said at a news conference that he doesn’t believe Trump is uncomfortable with Canada furthering its trade relationship with China. He said Trump has sought to understand where Canada is going in terms of trade ties with China.

Both leaders are attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the China’s tech hub, Shenzhen, where Canada and China agreed this week to drop trade restrictions on things like Canadian pork and some Chinese steel.

Canada is set to send a trade mission to China in 2027 and Carney brokered a deal with Xi in January to allow a limited number of Chinese electrical vehicles to be sold in Canada.

Carney said Wednesday it’s been easier for Ottawa to secure new trade arrangements with China because Canada’s trade relations south of the border are “much more complex.”

“The United States fundamentally changed its trade objectives and we are focused on getting the right deal for Canadians,” he said.

He added that Canada’s focused on exporting to China commodities such as iron and oil, rather than advanced sensitive technologies like superconductors.

RELATED: B.C. seafood harvesters say it’s super exciting Chinese tariffs are being lifted on their products

Diplomacy between Canada and the U.S. has been dicey as Trump hit Canada with heavy tariffs, and threatened repeatedly to turn Canada into the 51st state. They became more tense since Carney’s government walked away from formal trade talks in August, as Ottawa and Washington accused each other of pushing eleventh-hour changes.

Carney has said Trump’s team wanted to restrict Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries, endanger Canada’s protections for language and culture, and maintain hefty tariffs on some automobiles.

In response, Washington imposed tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods. Ottawa then followed up with retaliatory tariffs on American products.

Trump has long insisted Canada has treated the United States unfairly, despite the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement, also known as CUSMA, that was negotiated during his first term.

Carney has repeatedly said he will only agree to a deal if it is good for Canada.

“We will do what’s necessary in order to achieve that deal, but only that deal that is in the interests of Canadians,” he said.

Carney has also said trade talks with Washington would shape how Canada approaches Chinese investment, and that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if those talks fail.

Democrats have indicated that ending the trade war with Canada will be a top priority when they take the majority in Congress in January.

A University of Victoria athlete won her second straight U SPORTS cross-country championship over the weekend, and even set a course record.

Twenty-five-year-old Madelyn Eybergen, who’s nicknamed Mad Dog, covered the eight-kilometre route in just over 26 minutes – at a total of 26:05 minutes, beating out second place by more than 81 seconds.

It’s the second year in a row that Eybergen won gold at the national championship, completing the race with an average of 3:15 minutes per kilometre.

The competition also marked the second straight year that the UVic Vikes’ women’s cross-country team won the national championship, and the 11th time the program has won gold overall.

The U SPORTS national championship victory on Nov. 14 in Hamilton, Ont. means the Vikes’ women’s cross-country team is the second most successful team in the competition’s history, just behind the University of Guelph.

Meanwhile, Vikes cross-country head coach Hilary Stellingwerf was also named the U SPORTS Women’s Coach of the Year for a second consecutive year.

“I think their composure impressed me the most. They went out and got in position for where they needed to be which can be risky, but they held strong and even moved up,” said Stellingwerff in a release Saturday.

“Obviously Maddy put on a pretty special show, it was a pretty historical performance. I don’t think people realize it, but the pace and the time that she ran is unbelievable and I don’t think we’ve seen that in a long time, if ever, so it’s pretty special,” she said.

The weekend’s wins mark another feather in UVic’s athletics cap for the year. Over the same weekend, the Vikes men’s soccer team won their first U SPORTS national championship in 15 years in a dramatic 1-0 overtime victory over the University of Montreal Sunday.

A week before that, the Vikes women’s rugby team won their first-ever national title in a blowout game against the University of Victoria.

]]> 1362180 Researchers on B.C. coast use drones to collect whale snot for genome sequencing https://cheknews.ca/researchers-on-b-c-coast-use-drones-to-collect-whale-snot-for-genome-sequencing-1362165/ Wed, 18 Nov 2026 15:30:00 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1362165

Researchers studying humpback whales off the coast of British Columbia used drones to collect "whale snot," allowing scientists to conduct a complete genome sequencing without darts, biopsies or approaching closely with a boat.

The post Researchers on B.C. coast use drones to collect whale snot for genome sequencing appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

Researchers studying humpback whales off the coast of British Columbia used drones to collect “whale snot,” allowing scientists to conduct a complete genome sequencing without darts, biopsies or approaching closely with a boat.

Eadin O’Mahony, lead researcher in the study published in the scientific journal Molecular Ecology Resources this week, said her team spent 2022 and 2023 collecting the samples.

“It was (about) getting the whole genome, but it was getting a whole genome in a non-invasive way,” she said of the project.

Genomic data is an important tool for conservation, she said, letting researchers measure population health, including genetic diversity and inbreeding, and helping them identify individuals and estimate population size.

“To have an understanding of the genetic resilience of a population of animals is really important for their long-term protection, their conservation,” O’Mahony said in an interview from Cork, Ireland.

To collect the DNA, she would pilot a drone from a small vessel or from land at the Fin Island Research Station in a remote location on B.C.’s northern coast. 

Humpback whales forage in the region in the summer before migrating to Hawaii to breed in the winter, she said. 

The drone flights were conducted under a Fisheries and Oceans Canada research permit.

O’Mahony said she would be watching through the video feed to ensure the animal was not visually showing any signs of distress as she approached. If any were detected, they would terminate the flight, she said, adding this happened “very rarely.”

The drone carried a sterile petri dish and would hover over the whale, waiting for it to take the typical five to six breaths per surfacing.

“I’m trying to pre-empt the whale’s behaviour somewhat positioning the drone just behind the blowhole so that when she comes up to take that exhale, I’m ready to just fly through the breath covering the petri dishes in these little ‘mucusy’ droplets that’s what is effectively snot,” O’Mahony said.

The drone would then capture a photo of the animal’s tail fluke as it dove below the water’s surface. 

She said the tail fluke is similar to a “human fingerprint,” allowing scientists to easily identify each animal. 

A second photographer would use a zoom camera to help ensure a “fluke ID photograph” is captured during each collection.

“The actual sampling event is very quick,” she said, noting each flight only takes a couple of minutes.

“The scientific study, on the other hand — science is a slow game,” she said.

They collected 58 blow samples from a total of 26 humpbacks. The study said about 84 per cent of the DNA in the blow came from the whale itself. 

Repeat samples from the same whales, collected in different encounters and across the two years, gave matching genomes. Blow genomes also matched previously collected biopsy genomes from the same animals, the study said.

Researchers, alongside collaborators from the Globe Institute at the University of Copenhagen, the North Coast Cetacean Society and Fisheries and Oceans Canada, also discovered genetic diversity estimated from blow samples was very similar to those of traditional biopsies. 

The customary way of obtaining a genetic sample is from a biopsy, which requires getting a boat very close to the animal to dart it to obtain pieces of the whale’s blubber and skin. 

The research also determined the population studied shows little evidence of recent inbreeding.

O’Mahony said the humpback whale population declined about 20 per cent between 2012 and 2021, which she called “quite significant and quite worrying.”

“Genetic understanding helps us make management plans for our conservation agencies, to make management plans that are sustainable and protect these animals going forward,” she said.

O’Mahony noted humpbacks were long subjects of commercial hunts, which “brought their numbers to the brink of extinction.” 

She said there has been local recovery along B.C.’s coast, but there are conservation concerns over more expanded vessel traffic from tankers in the region, which increases the chances of fatal ship strikes.

“Getting that baseline information on what their genetic health looks like is really important in that context,” O’Mahony said.

She said there are scenarios where biopsy sampling is not possible, so this provides a non-invasive alternative.

“It’s not so much that the blow sampling will once and for all replace biopsy sampling, but there are a number of places where the blow sampling has its place,” she said.

“It just opens the door to more scenarios in which we might need to get the genetic material, but we haven’t been able to get it to such quality up until this point.”

She said she thinks blow sampling data is “only going to get better from here.”

“This is not the end of the road,” she said.

“It’s just going to open the door to increasingly non-invasive methods of research for conservation genomics.”

Canadians across the country can expect to hear the shrill screeching sound of Canada’s emergency alerting system today.

Pelmorex, which operates the Alert Ready system, says a test message and tone will be broadcast on television, radio and compatible wireless devices.

It says test messages will be issued in every province and territory at specific times between morning and early afternoon.

The system is usually tested in May and November and is part of Canada’s effort to ensure it works and raises awareness.

There is no option to opt out of the test or actual emergency alerts.

The Alert Ready system issued 1,215 alerts in Canada as of Oct. 31, for emergencies including Amber Alerts, tornadoes and thunderstorms.

BOGOTA, Colombia (AP) — A rare encounter between Indigenous people living in isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest and members of a neighboring community has prompted government protections amid concerns about the group’s health and threats to its forest home.

The encounter began Monday near a government access control post and the Guajajara Indigenous village of Tawari in the northeastern state of Maranhao, according to a statement Tuesday from Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples.

The ministry said around 20 members of the isolated Awa people had been sighted approaching the area in the Arariboia Indigenous Territory, but cautioned that information remained preliminary as authorities assessed the situation. The encounter has raised concerns about why members of a group that has spent decades hunting, fishing and gathering food while avoiding outsiders would suddenly approach a neighboring community, particularly as illegal logging, hunting and other intrusions threaten their forest territory. Images of the encounter have also drawn widespread attention.

Sarah Shenker, head of Survival Brasil, part of Survival International, an organization that advocates for Indigenous peoples’ rights, called the encounter “a crisis moment really and a wake-up call,” urging Brazilian authorities to crack down on illegal intrusions into Awa territory.

She said the images could help reinforce the existence of isolated Indigenous groups, whose presence is sometimes disputed by those seeking access to their lands. But she warned that the circumstances surrounding the encounter were troubling.

An unusual encounter with the isolated Awa people documented

Footage recorded by members of the neighboring Guajajara Indigenous community and shared by Survival International shows Awa adults and children gathered amid dense vegetation, some carrying bows and arrows and wearing feathered headdresses and necklaces.

The reason for the group’s approach remains unclear, but Survival International says the Awa apparently approached a government team, asked for yams and took them back into the forest.

The Arariboia territory has faced decades of pressure from illegal intruders, Shenker said, leaving isolated communities increasingly vulnerable as surrounding forests have been cleared.

The Brazilian government said the Awa group is already registered in the official database of isolated Indigenous peoples and is monitored by a specialized protection team from Funai, the federal Indigenous affairs agency. Funai personnel and Indigenous health workers are now in the area, and authorities have activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess potential contact situations and health risks.

Survival International has previously estimated that around 100 Awa remain uncontacted, although that is not necessarily a current population count. Other Awa live in settled villages and maintain contact with outsiders.

Fears for the tribe’s safety

One of the most immediate concerns is the risk of disease. Indigenous peoples living in isolation can be particularly vulnerable to infectious illnesses because of their limited previous exposure to pathogens common in the wider population.

The ministry stressed that its policy is not to encourage contact, but to protect the Awa’s right to remain isolated and determine for themselves whether to establish relations with outsiders. It also cautioned that a brief encounter does not necessarily mean a group has abandoned its isolation or chosen to establish permanent contact.

The Arariboia territory is also home to the Guajajara people, whose Indigenous forest guardians have spent years monitoring their lands and confronting illegal intrusions.

Shenker said those efforts have led to violence against the community, including killings of some community members, while responsibility for protecting the territory ultimately rests with the Brazilian government.

“The only way that they will survive is if intruders are kept out of their forest once and for all,” she said.

Despite the attention generated by the rare images, Shenker said she would rather the Awa had remained out of sight, living undisturbed in their forest.

“We would rather not have images and not have video footage of the uncontacted Awa when that means that they are living in the way that they choose in their forest, able to get on with their lives, hunting, fishing, gathering,” she said.

Two Vancouver Island athletes are among 35 who were selected to receive funding and training to help pursue their dreams of competing at the Olympics, following the 2026 RBC Training Ground National Final in Mississauga.

The competition took place on Oct. 3, and this week the RBC Training Ground program announced the 35 winners out of 100 participants, including Campbell River’s Cameron Meldrum and Nanaimo’s Sophia Ledingham.

The RBC Training Ground is an annual program run in partnership with the Canadian Olympic Committee and regional Canadian Sport Institutes that brings together top athletes from across the country for an Olympic talent search.

Winners then receive support for their training, including funding, mentorship, coaching, networking and other resources.

Meldrum sets eyes on winter sports

Scouts at the competition say Meldrum, 17, is a rising star when it comes to some winter sports.

He’s considered one of the fastest skate skiers in the country for his age group and has a varied sports history that could benefit his future pursuits, scouts say.

“Cameron is a strong cross country skier and mountain biker who has now also become interested in competing in biathlon,” said Clayton Whitman, performance pathway director at Biathlon Canada. 

“His skiing ability and training background make him a promising athlete as he aims for Canada Winter Games and a place on Biathlon Canada’s NextGen Team in the future.”

Funding from the RBC Training Ground program will be used for things like a new, high-quality biathlon rifle and for competition costs like travelling.

“Cameron shows a lot of potential in the sport of biathlon and has started training in biathlon with his local biathlon club on Vancouver Island this season,” said Whitman. “Given his ski speed, he is expected to qualify for our 2027-2028 U21 NextGen team in his first year of competing in biathlon. This will open up opportunities for him to represent Canada on the Junior IBU Cup circuit that season.”

Sophia Ledingham at home in the water

Meanwhile, 21-year-old Sophia Ledingham impressed scouts at the RBC Training Ground finals in the sport of rowing.

Previously a swimming athlete with the Nanaimo Riptides and a member of the Vancouver Island Biathlon Club, Ledingham has made a mark pivoting to rowing at the University of Calgary.

“We could see Sophia’s great aerobic sports background, in swimming and biathlon, in her Assault bike and Erg scores,” said Chuck McDiarmid, high performance manager with Rowing Canada. 

“Sophia started rowing in fall 2025 as a novice with the University of Calgary, and really her first time on water was spring 2026. Yet this summer she raced a very strong performance in the 2- at Canadian Henley, and will race for Dino’s at the Canadian University Championships,” he said.

The RBC Training Ground program first started in 2016, and has since gone on to help 28 Canadian athletes compete in four Olympic Games, winning 14 medals for the country.

Among those athletes is Campbell River’s Avalon Wasteneys who attended an RBC Training Ground in 2017 and became the first Olympian from the program to earn a medal – a gold medal in rowing at the Tokyo 2020 Games.

]]>

Coming off its first summer, Pumpty Dumpty, a boat tailor-made to clean up the waters of Brentwood Bay and the Tod Inlet, is gaining popularity.

Pumpty Dumpty is a mobile sani-pump service that’s operated by volunteers with a mission to improve the water quality of the Salish Sea. The not-for-profit program is a partnership between W̱JOȽEȽP Tsartlip First Nations, who own the boat, the Saanich Inlet Clean Waters Society (SICWS), who provide the pump-out service, and BC Ferries, who provides the discharge station for free. 

The 130-horsepower vessel patrols Brentwood Bay looking for boaters who need a sewage pump-and-dump. Its unique whistle also alerts boaters that they’re open for business. Pumpty Dumpty’s hull can hold up to 250 litres of sewage. Once full, it motors to the discharge station near the BC Ferries Brentwood Bay terminal to discharge the waste. The material then enters the municipal sewage system.

The volunteer-run service launched in May 2026 and, in its first four months, it has kept roughly 6,000 litres of sewage out of the waters that touch Brentwood Bay, Butchart Gardens and the Tod Inlet. That’s the equivalent of four standard-sized truck beds, or 40 standard bathtubs.

In its first four months, it removed sewage from 74 different mariners, some return customers, some new. 

“We’ve had absolutely fantastic support, and even those who don’t need a pump-out go, ‘Oh, we’re so glad you’re back and doing this,” says John Harper, president of SICWS.

Daryl Henry has moored his liveaboard at the Portside Marina for the past two years. Prior to Pumpty Dumpty, it would take Henry half a day to discharge his sewage. 

“Now I don’t have to go to Mill Bay and pump out and then come back. So it saves me a lot of time, so it’s nice if they just kinda show up and provide the service,” says Henry.

With Pumpty Dumpty, the whole service from tip to tail takes about 10 minutes or less.

Other service users include mariners on liveboards at Portside Marina, anglers, fireworks observers, day trippers and even vacationers from the U.S.

The program is picking up steam with boaters, but the long-term mission goes deeper still.

“The whole objective is we all have an interest in keeping the bay clean and healthy,” said Harper.

Will Morris, Tsartlip First Nation Stewardship director, has been working to clean up the waters for decades.

“We’ve managed to degrade the situation so bad that we can’t eat the shellfish…we can’t practice our traditional ways, so we’re just trying to create a better situation for not only our generation but future generations,” said Will Morris, Tsartlip First Nation Stewardship director.

Over the years, there have been numerous attempts from different operators to provide the service, but it hasn’t managed to stay afloat. It’s been nearly five years since the program has run in the bay, and with an increasing number of boaters in the area, it’s a cause that Harper and Morris are focused on.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

In the early 2000s, Harper helped operate a similar service in the Bay until 2015, after Butchart Gardens started operating its own pump-out boat for the area. That ended in 2022. 

That’s when Butchart Gardens gifted the boat to Tsartlip First Nation, encouraging the Tsartlip Stewardship Marine team to carry on the work. But the stewardship team lacked the resources to operate another program. A number of clean-up initiatives were in motion, including water quality sampling, garbage clean-ups and efforts to remove derelict boats. Years later, the Tsartlip Stewardship Marine team continues to push for cleaner waters, organizing or partnering on regular clean-ups, like the upcoming event from Nov. 16-20. 

So when Harper and Morris agreed to partner up, work got underway to get Pumpty Dumpty afloat.

And many more hands have led to Pumpty Dumpty’s success.

The municipality has provided grant funding, Portside Marina provides free moorage for the vessel, and BC Ferries provides the discharge station at no cost.

In an email to CHEK this month, BC Ferries said the “partnership has gone well, and we’ve been pleased to see the service run so smoothly.”

It adds that “BC Ferries is proud to support this initiative and the community’s efforts to help protect the health of Saanich Inlet and appreciate the work that they’re doing for the local community.”

Both Morris and Harper are focused on making Pumpty Dumpty sustainable, so plans for expansion are modest. Pumpty Dumpty is a free service that operates on grants and donations. Moving into the winter months, the volunteer-run program may have reduced operating hours, but will continue year-round. Boaters can book the service online. Harper says they may try to hire one staff member to keep up with an expected busy summer in 2027.

You can learn more at PumptyDumpty.ca.

B.C.’s seafood harvesters, including many here on Vancouver Island, are breathing a sigh of relief tonight after an announcement out of China.

The federal government has struck a deal with the Chinese government that will see tariffs on certain products from both countries dropped at the end of the year.

Chinese tariffs of 25 per cent, implemented in March 2024, on geoducks, sea cucumbers and shrimp will end.

Prime Minister Marc Carney arrived in China this week for the APEC Summit, a meeting of Pacific nation leaders, but in a face-to-face meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping before it started showed a sign that relations with the Communist regime are continuing to thaw.

The Chinese are dropping tariffs in a number of areas, including a 25 percent tariff on geoducks, sea cucumbers and Pacific spot prawns, in exchange for a drop in Canadian tariffs on some vehicle imports and steel.

On Vancouver Island there’s huge relief among seafood harvesters with the tariffs on geoducks, sea cumbers and prawns being dropped at the end of 2026.

Watch the story below:

Loading the player...

“Probably the first time in almost two years that we can breathe a sigh of relief,” said Katie Lindsay, marketing director of the Geoduck Underwater Harvesters Association. “This is something that we’ve been advocating for every single day since March 2025. We just got back from a two-and-a-half-week trip in China meeting with both Canadian and Chinese officials.”

“Yeah it’s super exciting,” said Bonnie Dennis.

The Chinese tariffs were stifling for Canadian seafood producers that needed to fish their quota and try to maintain their customers.

“It reduces our price that we obtain at this end quite a bit. Who benefits from tariffs, I don’t quite know, certainly not the end user and certainly not the harvesters,” said George Dennis, the owner of Star Fleet Diving and co-founder of Fan Seafoods.

China represents the vast majority of B.C.’s geoduck and sea cucumber market. The $60 million per year geoduck industry was down about $15 million last year.

“Just by efforts for diversification and new projects I would say everybody lost money, and that’s related to higher labour costs, more expenses. Our fuel-related expenses have gone crazy just trying to make these businesses viable,” said Bonnie Dennis, manager of Fan Seafoods and board member with the Pacific Sea Cucumber Harvesters Association.

The geoduck and sea cucumber market hits its peak demand during Chinese Lunar New Year celebrations. Producers are now trying to make the most of their fishing opportunities to end the year and prepare for the coming tariff removal.
